clinicalPearls: The congenital form is autosomal recessive, caused by loss-of-function SLC10A2 mutations affecting the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT/IBAT) of the terminal ileum.
It presents in infancy with chronic watery and fatty diarrhoea, faltering growth and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Interruption of the enterohepatic circulation depletes the bile acid pool and characteristically lowers plasma cholesterol, a useful clue that distinguishes it from other congenital diarrhoeas.
Bile acids spilling into the colon drive a secretory diarrhoea, so symptoms typically improve with a bile-acid sequestrant.
The far commoner adult 'primary' (type 2) bile acid diarrhoea is idiopathic and linked to impaired ileal FGF19 feedback with hepatic bile acid overproduction, not to ASBT loss.
SeHCAT (selenium-75 homotaurocholic acid) retention testing quantifies bile acid malabsorption; serum C4 (7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one) tends to be raised and FGF19 low.
An empirical trial of a bile-acid sequestrant is both diagnostic and therapeutic in the adult idiopathic form; fat-soluble vitamin status must be monitored in the congenital form.
reference.pathophysiology: In its congenital form, primary bile acid malabsorption is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in SLC10A2, encoding the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT, also called IBAT) expressed on the brush border of terminal ileal enterocytes, which mediates active reabsorption of conjugated bile acids. Failure of ileal uptake interrupts the enterohepatic circulation, delivering excess bile acids to the colon where they stimulate secretion and motility to produce a choleretic secretory diarrhoea, while compensatory upregulation of hepatic bile acid synthesis fails to restore the pool, causing fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption and low plasma cholesterol. The more common adult idiopathic (type 2) bile acid diarrhoea instead reflects impaired ileal FGF19 negative feedback on hepatic CYP7A1, so bile acid overproduction overwhelms normal reabsorptive capacity.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital chloride diarrhoea and congenital sodium diarrhoea
Microvillus inclusion disease and tufting enteropathy
Inborn errors of bile acid synthesis and metabolism
Secondary bile acid malabsorption from ileal Crohn's disease or resection
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (e.g. cystic fibrosis, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Faecal bile acid measurement and faecal fat estimation
Fat-soluble vitamin levels and plasma cholesterol
Therapeutic trial of a bile-acid sequestrant
Ileocolonoscopy and cross-sectional imaging to exclude secondary causes
redFlags: Severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance in an infant
Faltering growth or failure to thrive
Signs of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (bleeding tendency, rickets, neurological features)
New-onset bile acid diarrhoea with alarm features such as weight loss or bleeding, requiring exclusion of ileal Crohn's disease or malignancy
reference.prognosis: The congenital form usually responds symptomatically to bile-acid sequestrants but needs lifelong attention to fat-soluble vitamin status; the adult idiopathic form is generally benign and controllable, though frequently under-recognised and chronic.
pitfalls: Labelling idiopathic bile acid diarrhoea as diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome and never testing for or treating bile acid malabsorption.
Assuming all bile acid malabsorption is secondary to ileal disease and overlooking the primary and congenital forms.
In infants, missing complications of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Forgetting that bile-acid sequestrants bind co-administered drugs and fat-soluble vitamins, so dose timing must be separated.
